strengths: The paper addresses a clear clinical NLP resource gap with an openly released synthetic corpus covering 14 SBDH categories plus pain, including spans, status, temporality, and rationales. Its accessibility and broader category coverage offer practical value.

The central claim that synthetic supervision can improve compact SBDH classifiers is supported by experiments across model families and two clinical datasets. For example, RoBERTa macro-F improves from 55.64 to 91.11 on MIMIC-SBDH with prompt-based training and from 72.38 to 80.71 on VA-SBDH with standard training. Three-run reporting and category-specific analyses strengthen this evidence.

The expert review of 1,755 synthetic examples is substantial. Experienced annotators, adjudication, explicit correction procedures, and detailed error analysis support the resource's usefulness. The provided seed examples, generation prompt, filtering threshold, category mappings, and training configurations also support reuse. Together, these contributions warrant Findings publication.
weaknesses: The breadth and magnitude of improvement require qualification. In Table 4, encoder NER gains are negligible, while the large T5 improvement starts from a highly unstable baseline and still underperforms baseline RoBERTa. VA-SBDH classification gains are also absent for some models. The highlighted 94.44-point housing improvement involves only 18 positive test examples. Moreover, evaluation includes target-domain fine-tuning, establishing useful initialization across settings rather than transfer without local supervision.

The experiments do not adequately distinguish benefits of synthetic content from additional optimization and improved category balance. Appendix D.2 provides a useful training-step-matched comparison, but MIMIC-SBDH covers fewer categories than Synth-SBDH. Matched resampling or class-reweighting controls and better investigation of the unstable T5 baseline would clarify the source of the gains.

Several distinctive resource features receive limited validation. Appendix C.1 restricts experiments to positive annotations, and temporality is not evaluated as a prediction target. Rationale distillation is tested only on synthetic text, with macro-F gains of 0.66 and 0.58 points; the FLAN-T5 result is nonsignificant (P=0.36). This supports a limited auxiliary-supervision result, not the stronger conclusion that reasoning capability transfers to clinical extraction.

The annotation audit reveals meaningful residual limitations: experts corrected 286 annotations, discarded 142, and added 581 missing annotations. The same experts supplied seeds and reviewed visible GPT-4 annotations, leaving possible anchoring effects unmeasured. The 71.06% agreement uses relaxed span matching and does not establish exact-span or attribute-specific reliability. These issues qualify the high-quality benchmark claim, although they do not invalidate the demonstrated training utility.

Reproducibility and reporting need clarification. VA-SBDH is private, and the manuscript omits downstream prompt templates/verbalizers and generation decoding settings. The stated split sizes sum to 8,727 rather than 8,767. Table 14 also repeats the ClinicalMamba baseline means and deviations from Table 3 for Llama 3.2, warranting verification. These reporting gaps and the limited validation of the broader claims constrain the main-conference case.
